prompt.context: Our client is a large financial services firm with multiple locations around the world. Part of their service offering includes a 24-hour helpline. The client has their call centers in New York and Paris. The client has recently acquired a small firm (Firm B) in order to expand its reach in a particular geography. Firm B provides a subset of the services and has its call center located in the Philippines.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to determine its strategy going forward for handling customer calls. In particular they want us to look into the call center operations. The client wants any proposed solution to be cash neutral by the end of year 2.

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client provide?
clarifying_info.a: The client provides the full range of financial services for individuals and small organizations.

clarifying_info.q: How established is the acquired firm?
clarifying_info.a: Firm B was started 5 years ago and is still run by the original founders.

clarifying_info.q: What are the staffing requirements for call center employees?
clarifying_info.a: New employees are college graduates with basic knowledge of financial services and products. Fluency in English and several European languages is required.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any regulatory constraints in the existing locations?
clarifying_info.a: It is very difficult to lay off employees in the Paris location and significant costs will be incurred. The Philippines government encourages investment in the country and significant tax advantages are possible.

clarifying_info.q: Are the call centers currently operating at capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all call centers are currently operating at full capacity.

clarifying_info.q: Is there space and infrastructure to expand the Philippines facility?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, space and infrastructure necessary to expand is currently available. Assume overhead is variable.

exhibits.title: Call center performance – FY2010
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three call center locations (New York, Paris, Philippines) on four metrics: calls per year, employee cost per year ($), overhead cost per year ($), and number of employees.

framework: Options analysis: (1) No changes – maintain all 3 call centers; (2) Close Firm B's Philippines call center and route calls to NY or Paris; (3) Consolidate all calls to a single location (Philippines)
Company / call center comparison: compare services offered, product mix, and performance metrics (cost per call, calls per rep) across all three locations
Cost structure: evaluate current total costs and potential cost structure under each option, including one-time transition costs
Outsourcing-specific concerns: employment regulations (especially Paris layoffs), quality of calls, infrastructure capabilities, cultural/language fit, reputational risk
Client constraint: any solution must be cash neutral by end of year 2

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total current cost incurred by both firms and derive the calls-per-employee and cost-per-call for each location.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply employee cost by headcount and add overhead to get total cost per location, then sum. Derive efficiency ratios to compare locations.

math.setup: Total cost = (employee cost/year * # employees) + overhead cost/year. Calls/employee/year = calls/year / # employees. Cost/call = total cost / calls/year.
math.answer: Total combined cost = $9.6M. Philippines has the lowest cost per call ($6) but operates at half the efficiency of NY in calls per employee (4,000 vs 8,000).

questions.prompt: If we consolidate all calls to the Philippines at its current efficiency (4,000 calls/employee/year), how many employees are needed and what is the new total operating cost? Does this meet the two-year cash-neutral requirement given a one-time transition cost of $5M?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate headcount needed for total call volume (NY + Paris + Philippines = 1.3M calls), compute new operating cost, compare savings to one-time cost over two years.

math.setup: Total calls = 600,000 + 400,000 + 300,000 = 1,300,000. Employees needed = total calls / 4,000. New total cost = employees * $20,000 + overhead (variable, scales proportionally: $300,000/75 employees * new employees).
steps: Overhead scales: original OH per call = 300,000 / 300,000 = $1/call; new OH = 1,300,000 * 1 = $1,300,000
math.answer: Operating cost = $7.8M (savings of $1.8M/year). But with a $5M one-time cost, two-year cumulative savings ($3.6M) do not cover the investment. The move is NOT profitable within 2 years at current Philippines efficiency.

questions.prompt: What if Philippines employees can be trained to match New York's efficiency (8,000 calls/employee/year) within 3-6 months? Recalculate the headcount, costs, and check two-year cash neutrality. (Assume overheads double due to better equipment needed.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate at higher efficiency, note overhead assumption, compute new total cost, annual savings, and compare to $5M one-time cost over two years. Should also raise qualitative concerns about feasibility.

math.setup: At NY efficiency: employees needed = 1,300,000 / 8,000. New OH doubles from original Philippines OH level of $1.3M to $2.6M. New total cost = employees * $20,000 + $2,600,000. One-time cost still $5M.
math.answer: New total operating cost = $5.8M, saving $3.8M/year. Two-year cumulative savings of $7.6M exceed the $5M one-time cost, achieving cash neutrality within year 2. This is $2M better than the pre-efficiency-improvement scenario.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative concerns and risks must the client address when deciding whether to consolidate operations to the Philippines?

categories.name: Talent and workforce
ideas: Can the client hire ~160 qualified, English/European-language-fluent college graduates in the Philippines within the required time frame?
Will best practices from NY and Paris transfer successfully within 3-6 months?
Knowledge gaps during transition could hurt service quality

categories.name: Regulatory and legal
ideas: Significant layoff costs in Paris due to strict employment laws
Speed of NY staff reduction is uncertain and may delay savings
Philippines tax incentives could offset some one-time costs

categories.name: Service quality and customer satisfaction
ideas: Will customers notice a difference in service quality with the new labor base?
Financial services clients may be sensitive to accent or communication differences
Potential for increased call escalations during ramp-up period

categories.name: Reputational and competitive risk
ideas: Public backlash from large-scale outsourcing of jobs from NY and Paris
Competitors could leverage reputational damage to steal customers
Brand perception as a global financial firm may be affected

categories.name: Organizational and cultural integration
ideas: Firm B is still run by original founders – cultural integration with the parent is not yet complete
Scaling from 75 to 160 employees in Philippines changes the nature of the acquired organization
Aligning processes and systems across previously separate entities takes time

recommendation: Recommend consolidating call center operations to the Philippines, provided the client can achieve NY-level efficiency (8,000 calls/employee/year) within 3-6 months through best-practice transfer. This yields $3.8M in annual savings against a $5M one-time cost, achieving cash neutrality before end of year 2.

If efficiency improvement cannot be reliably achieved, consolidation at current Philippines efficiency does not meet the two-year cash-neutral requirement and the client should consider a hybrid approach (e.g., close only Paris, route volume to NY and Philippines).
risks: Risk of not finding ~160 qualified, multilingual graduates quickly enough in the Philippines
Service quality degradation during transition could lead to customer churn
Paris layoff process may be slow and costly, delaying the realization of savings
Significant scaling (75 to ~160 employees) creates organizational strain in an already recently acquired entity
Reputational damage from high-profile outsourcing decision in NY and Paris
next_steps: Analyze Philippines infrastructure requirements and capacity to confirm physical expansion feasibility
Develop a detailed talent acquisition and training plan for ~160 new Philippines hires
Quantify Paris severance costs more precisely to refine the $5M one-time estimate
Design a best-practices transfer program with clear milestones and quality checkpoints
Model customer satisfaction impact and prepare a stakeholder communication plan for NY and Paris staff
